column2: In Hungary the spaced pile wall has spread for tight urban excavations in very hard clay that do not reach the groundwater: the soil arches between the piles, few piles are enough. Sheet piles are hard to drive in hard clay, and the vibration endangers the neighbour.
Two-level underground car park in groundwater
An 8 m deep excavation in sandy gravel, groundwater 2 m below the surface, impermeable clay at 14 m. Old houses stand right on the plot boundary, anchoring is not possible.
Spaced pile wall as a cantilever

A watertight, stiff wall keyed into the impermeable clay is needed (diaphragm wall), with stiff support without anchors (the slabs acting as diaphragms). The soldier pile wall and the spaced pile wall are not watertight, and the vibration of sheet piling and the anchors are ruled out because of the neighbours.
Foundation of a new bridge pier in 6 m of water, in a sandy-gravelly river bed.
Single-wall braced sheet pile cofferdam + underwater concrete plug
Earth cofferdam with a clay core

For a bridge pier the typical solution is a braced sheet pile “box”: the bracing frame is also the template, and the weight of the underwater concrete plug holds against uplift. An earth cofferdam in such a depth of water would be very wide and would narrow the channel.
A 7 m deep temporary excavation on an open plot, high groundwater. The impermeable layer is 18 m deep – well below the toe the wall needs structurally. The wall will have to be removed later.

This is exactly the economical field of the slurry wall: high groundwater, a temporary excavation about 7–8 m deep, the quasi-watertight wall reaches the deep impermeable layer, but the steel beams only go to the depth needed structurally. The other solutions listed are not watertight.
Supporting a cutting beside a road
A 5 m high, almost vertical cutting in cohesive soil, no groundwater. A cheap, fast solution that can be modified flexibly is needed.

Soil nailing is relatively cheap, made with simple equipment, adapts well and can be modified. It works well in cohesive soil without groundwater; permanent use needs corrosion protection (epoxy, PE sheath).
Metro station in the city centre
A 25 m deep, 20 m wide excavation, dense surroundings, basements and utilities under the neighbours – anchors cannot be installed.
Diaphragm wall + steel tubular struts (at several levels)

Tubular struts are economical if anchoring is not possible (ground conditions, neighbouring underground spaces), or if the excavation is deeper than 15–20 m and, because of the neighbouring structures to be protected, a stiff enough wall cannot be built with anchors: the typical support system of metro stations. The diaphragm wall is watertight and stiff. Top-down can also work – what matters is stiff support without anchors.
Tunnel cross passage in saturated sand
A cross passage between two tunnel tubes, 18 m deep, in saturated sand – no wall can be built from the surface.

Frozen soil is watertight and load-bearing at the same time – temporarily, in almost any saturated soil, even with pipes drilled from the tunnel. It is expensive and slow, but here the other solutions cannot even be built.
Congratulations, you are a master excavation support designer!
Very good – the wrong ones are worth thinking through again.
It is worth going through the decision support and the chapters once more.
We would not build it this way.
Elements – tap them on the drawing too

Lines the soil face. Traditionally pine planks, so-called 2-inch (48 mm) thick, 5–6 m long; the end is protected from splitting by a steel strap. In stable, cohesive soil open planking is also possible: about every second plank is left out.
Holds the planks together and passes the earth pressure acting on them to the struts. A timber beam of 12–24 cm side length. Horizontal with vertical planking, vertical with horizontal planking.

Compression member: wedged between the two opposite walings, it braces the soil faces against each other – the earth pressures of the two sides “cancel out”. Round timber, 12–16 cm in diameter; it has to be checked for compression and buckling.
A pair of hardwood wedges between the end of the strut and the waling – used to tighten the strut. They have to be knocked tight before every shift.
A U-shaped steel dog between the strut and the waling: it stops the strut from falling out (compulsory for trenches wider than 1,5 m).

Thin-walled (3–6 mm) profiled steel sheet with an effective width of 25–30 cm: Patria and Union trench sheets, or CS corrugated sheets. The joints between the elements are not watertight – they are for shoring, not for keeping out water. They can be driven, vibrated and extracted.
Most often a hot-rolled I or U section; it holds the planks together and passes the load to the struts.

An adjustable-length strut: turning the middle tube extends the left- and right-hand threaded spindles at the two ends at the same time, so the strut can be tightened. It can also be an I-beam or a tube.
The head plate at the end of the screw strut: it presses against the waling, and the compressive force is transferred through it.

Cross-bracingThe pressure of the soil face is taken by the plank, collected by the waling, and the strut in compression passes it to the opposite side – where an equal earth pressure resists it. Tap an element!
m₀ = 0: the soil face does not stand for a moment without support (coarse-grained soil). The steel sheets are driven or vibrated in before excavation.
H ≤ m₀: the excavation can be dug to full depth, then it is lined with planks, walings and struts.
c) Horizontal planking, excavation in steps
H ≫ m₀, and m₀ is only a few decimetres: work proceeds in steps of m₀, with horizontal planks and vertical walings replaced generation by generation.
H > m₀: work proceeds downwards in steps of depth m₀, and after each step the planks are driven down to the new bottom.
E.g. soil stored at the edge, traffic; in design typically at least 10 kPa.
It must be shored in any case for occupational safety (H = ${fmt(H, 1)} m > ${fmt(L, 1)} m): the exposed soil face dries out, soaks up water, its condition deteriorates.
We are below the shoring limit (${fmt(L, 1)} m) – but with dynamic effects (traffic, piling) or near a building it has to be shored even then.
green: stands unsupported · red: support needed
m₀ as a function of cohesion (the other data fixed)
Condition: m₀ ≥ H – the excavation can be dug to full depth without support (cohesive soil, above the groundwater).
Excavation to full depth – possible because H < m₀: the vertical soil face stands for a short time.
The planks are set vertically against the soil faces: they line the face. In cohesive soil open planking is also possible – about every second plank is left out.
The walings holding them together are placed horizontally, at right angles to the planks.
The walings are braced against each other with struts and wedged – in at least two rows.
A protected working space: the pipe is placed in the free space below the struts.
Removal from the bottom up, keeping pace with the backfill (layers of 15–20 cm): a strut may only come out once compacted soil already supports the face below it. The planks are pulled out last.
Condition: H > m₀ – m₀ is significant (e.g. ~1 m), but smaller than the planned depth.
Excavation of the first step, to depth m₀.
The first frame is complete: the long planks still reach far above ground level, and a waling and strut are placed on them.
Excavation of the next step (another ~m₀): the ends of the planks now “hang” at the level of the old bottom.
The walings are temporarily supported, the wedges loosened, the planks driven down to the new bottom – then wedged again, and a new row of walings and struts is placed lower down.
Again support, driving down, a new row of struts – down to the final depth.
Complete: the planks cover the full depth, and their top ends stand about 20 cm above ground level (against soil falling in).
